lemmas.title: Component-wide relation

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The vector space of bivariate polynomials of total degree at most $87$ has dimension

$$\binom{89}{2}=3916,$$

so there are at most $p^{3916}$ candidates. Choose the values $f(x)$ independently and uniformly in $\mathbb F_p$. For a fixed candidate $Q$, its agreement count with $f$ has distribution $\operatorname{Bin}(p^2,1/p)$ and mean $p$. The moment bound gives

$$\Pr\bigl[|\{x:Q(x)=f(x)\}|\geq2p\bigr]\leq\left(\frac e4\right)^p<\left(\frac{11}{16}\right)^p.$$

Since

$$p<2^{18},\qquad \left(\frac{11}{16}\right)^2<\frac12,\qquad p=2\cdot73728+1,$$

and

$$18\cdot3916=70488<73728,$$

the union probability over all candidates is less than

$$2^{70488-73728}<1.$$

Thus some table $f$ agrees with every degree-at-most-$87$ bivariate polynomial on at most $2p-1$ points.

On each affine line, choose $88=d+1$ distinct points and interpolate the values of $f$ there by a univariate polynomial $P_L$ of degree at most $87$. This is valid because $88<147457$, so all Vandermonde denominators are nonzero. Each line has at least $88$ accepted points, and hence

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\geq\frac{88}{p}.$$

For the chosen $f$,

$$
\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f)
\leq\frac{2p-1}{p^2}
<\frac2p
<\frac{88}{10p}.
$$

This probabilistic-method argument proves the asserted witness.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$. Define

$$\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f):=\max_{\deg Q\leq87}\frac{|\{x\in\mathbb F_{147457}^{2}:Q(x)=f(x)\}|}{147457^2},$$

where the maximum is over bivariate polynomials of total degree at most $87$. There exist a table $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^{2}\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ and degree-at-most-$87$ line polynomials $(P_L)_L$ such that

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\geq\frac{88}{147457}$$

and

$$\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f)<\frac{2}{147457}<\frac{88}{10\cdot147457}.$$
lemmas.title: Random-table obstruction

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Every point of $\mathbb F_p^2$ lies on exactly one line in each of the $p+1$ directions. For lines in $\mathcal D$, the constant-zero polynomial agrees with $f$ at all $p$ points; for every other line, the constant-one polynomial agrees nowhere. Consequently, every point has exactly $939$ accepted incident lines, and the accepted lines are precisely the lines in the selected directions. Since every direction contains $p$ parallel lines,

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)=\frac{939p}{p(p+1)}=\frac{939}{147458}.$$

Moreover,

$$939p^2=20417209271211>20395544151487,$$

so

$$\frac{939}{147458}>\frac{20395544151487}{p^2(p+1)}=\varepsilon_*.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$, and set

$$\varepsilon_*:=\frac{20395544151487}{3206262880419842}.$$

Let $\mathcal D$ be any set of $939$ affine-line directions in $\mathbb F_{147457}^{2}$. Define $f(x):=0$ for every point and

$$
P_L:=
\begin{cases}
0,&\text{if the direction of }L\text{ lies in }\mathcal D,\\
1,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

Then

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)=\frac{939}{147458}>\varepsilon_*,$$

and every point has accepted degree exactly $939$.
lemmas.title: Direction concentration

lemmas.proof_markdown:
There are $p+1$ incidences between $X$ and $T$. Hence

$$a=\frac1{p^2},\qquad b=\frac1p,\qquad J(X,T)=\frac{p+1}{p^2(p+1)}=\frac1{p^2}.$$

Therefore

$$J(X,T)-ab=\frac1{p^2}-\frac1{p^3}=\frac{p-1}{p^3}.$$

Also,

$$
\frac{a(1-a)b(1-b)}{p+1}
=\frac{(p-1)^2}{p^6},
$$

so its square root is $(p-1)/p^3$. This gives equality in the centered incidence bound.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$. Let $X$ consist of one point of $\mathbb F_{147457}^{2}$, and let $T$ be the pencil of all $p+1$ affine lines through that point. Define

$$a:=\frac{|X|}{p^2},\qquad b:=\frac{|T|}{p(p+1)},$$

and

$$J(X,T):=\frac{|\{(x,L)\in X\times T:x\in L\}|}{p^2(p+1)}.$$

Then

$$J(X,T)-ab=\frac{p-1}{p^3}=\sqrt{\frac{a(1-a)b(1-b)}{p+1}}.$$
lemmas.title: Pencil extremizer

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Since $87668=87\cdot1007+59$, every exponent $k$ occurring in $V_D$ satisfies $k\le 1007<147457$. Thus characteristic pruning removes no monomial. Reversing the summation index gives

$$\dim V_D=\sum_{k=0}^{1007}\binom{87668-87k+2}{2}=\sum_{j=0}^{1007}\binom{87j+61}{2}.$$

Using

$$\sum_{j=0}^{1007}1=1008,\qquad \sum_{j=0}^{1007}j=507528,\qquad \sum_{j=0}^{1007}j^2=340889640,$$

we obtain

$$\dim V_D=\frac{7569(340889640)+10527(507528)+3660(1008)}{2}=1292770060848.$$

Substituting an affine parametrization and a polynomial of degree at most $87$ into a monomial of weighted degree at most $D$ produces a univariate polynomial of degree at most $D$. Each line identity therefore imposes at most $D+1=87669$ homogeneous linear conditions. Hence

$$\operatorname{rank}\Phi\le 14745800\cdot87669=1292749540200.$$

Rank-nullity yields

$$\dim\ker\Phi\ge1292770060848-1292749540200=20520648.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $m=2$, $p=147457$, $d=87$, $D=87668$, and $r_0=100(p+1)=14745800$. Define

$$V_D=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F_{147457}}\left\{X^iY^jZ^k:i,j,k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\ i+j+87k\le D\right\}.$$

For every set $R$ of $r_0$ distinct affine lines in $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$, every choice of affine parametrizations $L(t)$, and every family $p_L\in\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ with $\deg p_L\le87$, let

$$\Phi:V_D\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{L\in R}\mathbb F_{147457}[t]_{\le D},\qquad \Phi(A)=\bigl(A(L(t),p_L(t))\bigr)_{L\in R}.$$

Then

$$\dim V_D=1292770060848>1292749540200=r_0(D+1)$$

and

$$\dim\ker\Phi\ge20520648.$$
lemmas.title: Weighted monomial space

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The plane $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$ has

$$147457(147457+1)=21743714306>14745800$$

affine lines. If $|R|<14745800$, augment $R$ to a set $R'$ of exactly $14745800$ distinct affine lines and assign an arbitrary degree-at-most-$87$ polynomial label to each added line. The weighted-monomial count gives a kernel of dimension at least $20520648$ for the resulting restriction map. Any nonzero element $A$ of this kernel has weighted degree at most $87668$ and satisfies every formal identity indexed by $R'$. Discarding the added lines leaves all identities indexed by $R$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $m=2$, $p=147457$, and $d=87$. Let $R$ be a set of at most $14745800$ distinct affine lines in $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$. For every $L\in R$, fix an affine parametrization $L(t)$ and a polynomial $p_L\in\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ with $\deg p_L\le87$. Then there exists a nonzero polynomial $A\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ such that

$$\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(A)\le87668$$

and, for every $L\in R$,

$$A(L(t),p_L(t))=0\qquad\text{in }\mathbb F_{147457}[t].$$
lemmas.title: Fixed-instance interpolant

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Augment $R$ to a set $R'$ of exactly $14745800$ distinct affine lines and assign arbitrary degree-at-most-$87$ labels to the added lines. The interpolation lemma supplies a nonzero interpolant $A$ for $R'$.

Suppose that $A$ is independent of $Z$. For every $L\in R'$, the formal identity $A(L(t))=0$ implies that the affine-linear defining polynomial $\ell_L$ of $L$ divides $A$. Distinct affine lines have nonassociate irreducible defining polynomials, so

$$\prod_{L\in R'}\ell_L\mid A.$$

Consequently,

$$\deg A\ge |R'|=14745800,$$

contrary to $\deg A\le87668$. Thus $A$ depends on $Z$.

Every positive exponent $k$ of $Z$ in $A$ satisfies

$$1\le k\le\left\lfloor\frac{87668}{87}\right\rfloor=1007<147457.$$

Its derivative coefficient is therefore nonzero in $\mathbb F_{147457}$, and distinct monomials remain distinct after differentiation. Hence $A_Z\ne0$. Restricting the identities from $R'$ to $R$ proves the claim.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $m=2$, $p=147457$, and $d=87$. Let $R$ be a set of at most $14745800$ distinct affine lines in $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$. For every $L\in R$, fix an affine parametrization $L(t)$ and a polynomial $p_L\in\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ with $\deg p_L\le87$. Then there exists a nonzero polynomial $A\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ such that

$$\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(A)\le87668,\qquad A_Z\ne0,$$

and, for every $L\in R$,

$$A(L(t),p_L(t))=0\qquad\text{in }\mathbb F_{147457}[t].$$
lemmas.title: Formal differentiation

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Choose, among the interpolants supplied by the preceding lemma with nonzero $Z$-derivative, a polynomial $A$ of minimum weighted degree. Suppose that $A$ has a repeated irreducible factor, and write

$$A=F^eG,$$

where $F$ is irreducible, $e\ge2$, and $F\nmid G$. For each $L\in R$, set

$$F_L(t)=F(L(t),p_L(t)),\qquad G_L(t)=G(L(t),p_L(t)).$$

The identity $F_L^eG_L=0$ holds in the integral domain $\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$. Thus either $F_L=0$ or $G_L=0$, and consequently $F_LG_L=0$. Therefore $B=FG$ remains an interpolant.

Suppose that $B_Z=0$. Then

$$F_ZG+FG_Z=0.$$

Reduction modulo $F$ gives $F\mid F_ZG$. Since the polynomial ring is a unique factorization domain, $F$ is prime; because $F\nmid G$, it follows that $F\mid F_Z$. If $F_Z\ne0$, then $\deg_Z(F_Z)<\deg_Z(F)$, which is incompatible with this divisibility. Hence $F_Z=0$. The equality $B_Z=0$ then gives $G_Z=0$, and therefore

$$A_Z=eF^{e-1}F_ZG+F^eG_Z=0,$$

contrary to the choice of $A$. Thus $B_Z\ne0$.

Weighted degree is additive on products of nonzero polynomials. Since $F$ is nonconstant and $e\ge2$,

$$\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(B)<\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(A),$$

contradicting minimality. Hence $A$ has no repeated irreducible factor and is squarefree.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $m=2$, $p=147457$, and $d=87$. Let $R$ be a set of at most $14745800$ distinct affine lines in $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$. For every $L\in R$, fix an affine parametrization $L(t)$ and a polynomial $p_L\in\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ with $\deg p_L\le87$. Then there exists a nonzero squarefree polynomial $A\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ such that

$$\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(A)\le87668,\qquad A_Z\ne0,$$

and, for every $L\in R$,

$$A(L(t),p_L(t))=0\qquad\text{in }\mathbb F_{147457}[t].$$
lemmas.title: Squarefree reduction

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The inequality holds at $D=87668$ by the exact count in the weighted-monomial lemma. At $D=87667$,

$$N(D)=1292725845432,$$

whereas

$$14745800(D+1)=14745800\cdot87668=1292734794400.$$

The deficit is $8948968$.

Let $a_s$ be the number of supported monomials of exact weighted degree $s$. Multiplication by $X$ injects the layer of weight $s$ into the layer of weight $s+1$, so $(a_s)_{s\ge0}$ is nondecreasing. Consequently,

$$\frac{N(E)}{E+1}=\frac{1}{E+1}\sum_{s=0}^{E}a_s$$

is nondecreasing in $E$. For every $E\le87667$,

$$\frac{N(E)}{E+1}\le\frac{N(87667)}{87668}<14745800.$$

Thus no smaller degree satisfies the universal coefficient-count inequality. This establishes optimality only for that certificate; it does not rule out smaller interpolants for particular labeled-line data.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For $D\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, define

$$N(D)=\#\left\{(i,j,k)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^3:i+j+87k\le D,\ k=0\text{ or }147457\nmid k\right\}.$$

Then

$$\min\left\{D\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:N(D)>14745800(D+1)\right\}=87668.$$
lemmas.title: Coefficient-count threshold

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Exact counting at $d=87$ and $D=8700$ gives

$$\left|\mathcal N_{87,8700}\right|=\sum_{j=0}^{100}\binom{87j+2}{2}=1281144701.$$

The asserted lower bound evaluates to

$$\frac{8700^3}{3\cdot87}-\frac{5}{2}8700^2+\frac{8700\cdot87}{6}=2333901150.$$

This exceeds the exact count by $1052756449$. Hence the displayed inequality, and therefore HKSS v1 Claim A.4 as printed, is false at this specialization.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For positive integers $d$ and $D$, define

$$\mathcal N_{d,D}=\left\{(i,j,k)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^3:i+j+dk\le D\right\}.$$

At $d=87$ and $D=8700$,

$$\left|\mathcal N_{87,8700}\right|\ge\frac{8700^3}{3\cdot87}-\frac{5}{2}8700^2+\frac{8700\cdot87}{6}.$$
lemmas.title: HKSS specialization

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Let $q=\lfloor D/d\rfloor$, and let $\mathcal N_{d,D}$ denote the same set without the restriction on $k$. Then

$$\left|\mathcal N_{d,D}\right|=\sum_{k=0}^{q}\binom{D-dk+2}{2}\ge\frac12\sum_{k=0}^{q}(D-dk)^2.$$

The function $x\mapsto(D-dx)^2$ is nonnegative and decreasing on $[0,D/d]$. Therefore

$$\left|\mathcal N_{d,D}\right|\ge\frac12\int_0^{D/d}(D-dx)^2\,dx=\frac{D^3}{6d}.$$

Group the positive $Z$-exponents into blocks

$$\{ap+1,\ldots,(a+1)p\},\qquad a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.$$

Within every complete block, the excluded exponent $(a+1)p$ has the smallest monomial layer, so its contribution is at most $1/p$ of the block's contribution. A terminal incomplete block contains no excluded exponent, and the layer $k=0$ is retained. Hence

$$\left|\mathcal N_{d,D,p}\right|\ge\left(1-\frac1p\right)\left|\mathcal N_{d,D}\right|\ge\frac12\left|\mathcal N_{d,D}\right|\ge\frac{D^3}{12d}.$$

This proof does not use the refuted HKSS lower bound.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For $d\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}$, $D\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, and a prime $p\ge2$, define

$$\mathcal N_{d,D,p}=\left\{(i,j,k)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^3:i+j+dk\le D,\ k=0\text{ or }p\nmid k\right\}.$$

Then

$$\left|\mathcal N_{d,D,p}\right|\ge\frac{D^3}{12d}.$$
lemmas.title: Characteristic-pruned count

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Set

$$r_0=100(p+1)=14745800.$$

Then

$$87r_0=1282884600$$

and

$$35817^2=1282857489<87r_0<1282929124=35818^2.$$

The prescribed KTZ degree is therefore

$$16\left(\left\lfloor\sqrt{87r_0}\right\rfloor+1\right)=16(35817+1)=573088>147457.$$

Exact coefficient counting instead permits $D=87668<147457$, but the later requirements still fail. For every $0<\epsilon\le1$, let

$$k_1=\left\lfloor\frac{\epsilon p}{1000}\right\rfloor.$$

Then $k_1\le147$, so $D<k_1/2$ forces the integer $D\le73$. Any polynomial with $A_Z\ne0$ under the $(1,1,87)$ weighting has weighted degree at least $87$, which is incompatible with this requirement.

Moreover,

$$384^2<p+1<385^2,$$

so

$$\frac1{\sqrt{p+1}}>\frac1{385}>\frac1{8000}\ge\frac{\epsilon}{8000}.$$

Thus the required mixing inequality $1/\sqrt{p+1}\le\epsilon/8000$ also fails for every $0<\epsilon\le1$. Finally, the printed recovery bound $\epsilon/8000$ is weaker than the required bound $\epsilon/10$. Hence the printed fixed-instance slack chain cannot be instantiated. This does not refute the asymptotic KTZ theorem.

lemmas.title: KTZ slack specialization

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Set $p=147457$. By the pigeonhole principle, some $a\in\mathbb F_p$ satisfies

$$\left|\left\{x\in\mathbb F_p^2:f(x)=a\right\}\right|\ge\frac{p^2}{p}=p.$$

The constant polynomial $Q(X,Y)=a$ has total degree $0$, and

$$\Pr_{x\in\mathbb F_p^2}[Q(x)=f(x)]\ge\frac{p}{p^2}=\frac1{147457}>\frac1{10000000}=10^{-7}.$$

The hypothesis $\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\ge10^{-6}$ is unused, so the conclusion holds independently of acceptance.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ be a point table, and let $P$ assign to every affine line a univariate polynomial of degree at most $87$. If

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\ge10^{-6},$$

then there exists $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ such that

$$\Pr_{x\in\mathbb F_{147457}^2}[Q(x)=f(x)]\ge10^{-7}.$$
lemmas.title: Constant-polynomial agreement

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Set $p=147457$. The number of monomials $X^iY^j$ with $i+j\le87$ is

$$\binom{89}{2}=3916.$$

Consequently, there are at most $p^{3916}$ bivariate polynomials of total degree at most $87$. Choose every value $f(x)$ independently and uniformly from $\mathbb F_p$. For a fixed polynomial $Q$ of total degree at most $87$, let

$$X_Q=\left|\left\{x\in\mathbb F_p^2:Q(x)=f(x)\right\}\right|.$$

Then $X_Q$ is binomial with parameters $p^2$ and $1/p$, and

$$\mathbb E[2^{X_Q}]=\left(1-\frac1p+\frac2p\right)^{p^2}=\left(1+\frac1p\right)^{p^2}.$$

Markov's inequality gives

$$\Pr[X_Q\ge2p]\le\frac{(1+1/p)^{p^2}}{4^p}.$$

The standard exponential estimate gives $(1+1/p)^p<e$. Moreover,

$$e\le1+1+\frac12+\frac16+\frac1{24}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}4^{-j}=\frac{49}{18}<\frac{11}{4}.$$

It follows that

$$\Pr[X_Q\ge2p]<\left(\frac{11}{16}\right)^p.$$

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Choose a point table $f$ supplied by the preceding lemma and set $p=147457$. For every affine line $L$, fix an affine parametrization $L(t)$ and choose distinct elements

$$t_{L,1},\ldots,t_{L,88}\in\mathbb F_p.$$

This is possible because $88<p$. Define

$$P_L(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{88}f(L(t_{L,i}))\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le88\\j\ne i}}\frac{t-t_{L,j}}{t_{L,i}-t_{L,j}}.$$

All denominators are nonzero, and $P_L$ has degree at most $87$. It agrees with $f$ at the selected $88$ points of $L$. Under uniform line-then-point sampling,

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)=\frac1{p(p+1)}\sum_L\frac{\left|\left\{t\in\mathbb F_p:P_L(t)=f(L(t))\right\}\right|}{p}\ge\frac{88}{p}.$$

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\ge\frac{88}{p}\ge\epsilon$$

For $c=(f,(P_L)_{L\in\mathcal L})$, define $$A(c):=|\{(L,x):x\in L,\ P_L(x)=f(x)\}|$$ and $$G(f):=\max_{\deg Q\le87}|\{x\in X:Q(x)=f(x)\}|.$$ Thus $\operatorname{Pass}(c)=A(c)/N$, $\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f)=G(f)/M$, and $\operatorname{Sound}(\varepsilon)$ is $$\forall c,
\quad A(c)/N\ge\varepsilon\Longrightarrow G(f)/M\ge\varepsilon/10.$$

nodes.label: Exact integer cells
nodes.notes: The strict recovery failure and the open left endpoint are essential.
nodes.statement_markdown:
For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, let $$k=\lceil N\varepsilon\rceil,
\qquad r_k=\left\lfloor\frac{k-1}{H}\right\rfloor.$$ Then $$\left\lceil\frac{M\varepsilon}{10}\right\rceil=\left\lceil\frac{k}{H}\right\rceil$$ and $$\neg\operatorname{Sound}(\varepsilon)
\iff
\exists c:\ A(c)\ge k\ \land\ G(f)\le r_k.$$ Hence $\operatorname{Sound}$ is constant on $((k-1)/N,k/N]$.

nodes.label: Constant-polynomial integer certificate
nodes.notes: The cited source formally states only the $10^{-6}$ corollary; this node isolates the stronger pigeonhole fact proved inside it and therefore needs fresh exact-statement audit.
nodes.statement_markdown:
For $n_b(f):=|\{x\in X:f(x)=b\}|$, $$\sum_{b\in F}n_b(f)=M.$$ The integer system $$\sum_{b\in F}n_b=M,
\qquad 0\le n_b\le p-1$$ is infeasible because $$M=21743566849>p(p-1)=21743419392.$$ Consequently $G(f)\ge p=147457$ for every $f:X\to F$.

nodes.label: Universal low-score interval
nodes.notes: The acceptance hypothesis is unused; this is a defect of the literal score, not premise vacuity.
nodes.statement_markdown: For every rational $\varepsilon$ satisfying $$0<\varepsilon\le\frac{10}{147457},$$ one has $\operatorname{Sound}(\varepsilon)$.

nodes.label: No lowest positive soundness
nodes.notes: For example, every terminating decimal $10^{-j}$ with $j\ge5$ is a sound score.
nodes.statement_markdown: Let $$\mathcal S:=\{\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q:0<\varepsilon\le1\ \land\ \operatorname{Sound}(\varepsilon)\}.$$ Then $$\inf\mathcal S=0$$ and $\mathcal S$ has no least element.

nodes.label: Exact nonsound interval
nodes.notes: The witness is existential by the probabilistic method, not an explicit checker-accepted point table.
nodes.statement_markdown:
There exists $c=(f,P)$ such that $$A(c)\ge88\Lambda=1913446858928,
\qquad G(f)\le2p-1=294913.$$ Consequently $\neg\operatorname{Sound}(\varepsilon)$ for every $$\frac{20}{147457}\le\varepsilon\le\frac{88}{147457}.$$

nodes.label: Eliminate line-polynomial choices
nodes.notes: Each maximum is finite because a line label has exactly $88$ field coefficients.
nodes.statement_markdown:
For a fixed affine coordinate $t_L$ on each $L$, define $$\lambda_L(f):=\max_{c\in F^{88}}|\{x\in L:\sum_{j=0}^{87}c_jt_L(x)^j=f(x)\}|,
\qquad T(f):=\sum_{L\in\mathcal L}\lambda_L(f).$$

nodes.label: Independent line maximization
nodes.notes: There is no compatibility constraint between labels on distinct lines.
nodes.statement_markdown: For every $f:X\to F$, $$T(f)=\max_{(P_L)_{L\in\mathcal L}}A(f,(P_L)_L).$$

nodes.label: Exact bad-instance profile
nodes.notes: Adjoining $-1$ defines the maximum when the constrained set is empty.
nodes.statement_markdown: For $r\in\mathbb Z$, define $$C_r:=\max\left(\{-1\}\cup\{T(f):f:X\to F,\ G(f)\le r\}\right).$$

nodes.label: Soundness as one integer inequality
nodes.notes: Equivalently, each point table contributes the failure interval $(10G(f)/M,T(f)/N]$.
nodes.statement_markdown:
For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, with $k=\lceil N\varepsilon\rceil$ and $r_k=\lfloor(k-1)/H\rfloor$, $$\operatorname{Sound}(\varepsilon)
\iff C_{r_k}<k.$$

nodes.label: Reed–Muller coset normalization
nodes.notes: A formal proof must exhibit the triangular information set; the reduction is exact but still astronomically large.
nodes.statement_markdown:
Let $\mathcal C$ be the evaluation code of total-degree-at-most-$87$ bivariate polynomials and let $\mathcal C_L$ be the degree-at-most-$87$ Reed–Solomon code on $L$. Then $$G(f)=M-d_H(f,\mathcal C),
\qquad T(f)=N-\sum_{L\in\mathcal L}d_H(f|_L,\mathcal C_L).$$ Both quantities are invariant under $f\mapsto f+H$ for $H\in\mathcal C$. Since $\dim\mathcal C=\binom{89}{2}=3916$, an information set of size $3916$ gives each coset a unique representative vanishing on that set.

nodes.label: Exact finite bad-instance program
nodes.notes: The universal family of global-polynomial constraints is essential; replacing it by one existentially selected polynomial reverses the meaning.
nodes.statement_markdown:
For integers $k,r$, $\operatorname{BadIP}(k,r)$ is the finite $0$-$1$ system with one-hot variables $z_{x,b}$ for $f(x)=b$ and $u_{L,c}$ for the coefficient word $c\in F^{88}$ of $P_L$. Put $$v_{L,x,b}:=\sum_{c:\,P_c(t_L(x))=b}u_{L,c}$$ and impose $y_{L,x,b}=z_{x,b}\wedge v_{L,x,b}$ by its three exact linear inequalities. The remaining constraints are $$\sum_{L,x,b}y_{L,x,b}\ge k$$ and $$\sum_{x\in X}z_{x,Q(x)}\le r
\qquad\text{for every total-degree-at-most-$87$ polynomial }Q.$$

nodes.label: Integer-program semantics
nodes.notes: Both encoding directions must be audited against the canonical field and line enumerations.
nodes.statement_markdown:
For all integers $k,r$, $$\operatorname{BadIP}(k,r)\text{ is feasible}
\iff
\exists c:\ A(c)\ge k\ \land\ G(f)\le r
\iff C_r\ge k.$$

nodes.label: Finite exhaustive decision procedure
nodes.notes: This proves finite decidability, not practical tractability.
nodes.statement_markdown: Every $C_r$ is determined by enumerating exactly $p^{M-3916}$ normalized point-table representatives. For each representative, checking at most $p^{3916}$ global coefficient words and $\Lambda p^{88}$ line-label coefficient words determines $G(f)$ and $T(f)$. Thus every cell predicate $C_{r_k}<k$ is an exact finite obligation.

For $r_0=14745800$ and $D=87668$, the $(1,1,87)$-weighted monomial space has dimension $$1292770060848>r_0(D+1)=1292749540200,$$ while at $D=87667$ it has dimension $$1292725845432<1292734794400.$$ Every family of at most $r_0$ labeled affine lines therefore admits a nonzero squarefree interpolant $A$ with $$\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}A\le87668,
\qquad A_Z\ne0.$$

Let $$\varepsilon_1:=\frac{717920394295}{10^{12}}.$$ Then $$k_1:=\lceil N\varepsilon_1\rceil=2301841511324436,
\qquad r_1:=\left\lfloor\frac{k_1-1}{H}\right\rfloor=1561015008.$$ Therefore $$\operatorname{Sound}(\varepsilon_1)
\iff
\operatorname{BadIP}(k_1,r_1)\text{ is infeasible},$$ and soundness requires $G(f)\ge1561015009$ whenever $A(c)\ge k_1$.

Let $$k_2=20395544151487,
\qquad r_2=13831426.$$ Prove that every instance with $A(c)\ge k_2$ has a connected accepted core component containing at least $13831427$ points and a single polynomial $B$ of $(1,1,87)$-weighted degree at most $406$ such that $$B(x,f(x))=0,

With $\mathcal S$ as in `cc-no-least-score`, $$\mathcal S=\mathbb Q\cap\bigcup_{\substack{1\le k\le N\\ C_{\lfloor(k-1)/H\rfloor}<k}}\left(\frac{k-1}{N},\frac{k}{N}\right]$$ $$=\mathbb Q\cap\bigcup_{\substack{1\le k\le N\\ \operatorname{BadIP}(k,\lfloor(k-1)/H\rfloor)\text{ is infeasible}}}\left(\frac{k-1}{N},\frac{k}{N}\right].$$ Moreover, $$(0,10/147457]\cap\mathbb Q\subseteq\mathcal S,

nodes.statement_markdown: Set $F=\mathbb F_{147457}$, $\mathcal P=F^2$, let $\mathcal L$ be its affine lines, and let $\mathcal I=\{(x,L):x\in L\}$. Then $$M:=|\mathcal P|=21743566849,\qquad \Lambda:=|\mathcal L|=21743714306,\qquad J:=|\mathcal I|=3206262880419842.$$ For $f:\mathcal P\to F$ and $p_L\in F[t]$ with $\deg p_L\le87$, define $$E_{\rm acc}:=\{(x,L)\in\mathcal I:p_L(t_{L,x})=f(x)\},\qquad \operatorname{Pass}(f,P):=\frac{|E_{\rm acc}|}{J},$$ $$\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f):=\max_{\deg Q\le87}\Pr_{x\in\mathcal P}[Q(x)=f(x)].$$ Put $$D:=11915,\qquad K:=2299255117608635,\qquad \varepsilon_\star:=\frac KJ,\qquad \tau_\star:=\frac{\varepsilon_\star}{10}.$$

If $n=\deg_{G_0}(L)$, the summands defining $S_L$ are independent and $$\mathbb E[S_L]\ge n\bigl(1-(1-\theta)^{31647}\bigr).$$ For $s<\mathbb E[S_L]$, $$\Pr[S_L\le s]\le\exp\left(-\frac{2(\mathbb E[S_L]-s)^2}{n}\right).$$
